etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English aide, eide, ayde, from Old French eide, aide, from aidier, from Latin adiūtō, adiūtāre (“to assist, help”). Cognates include Spanish ayuda, Portuguese ajuda and Italian aiuto.

quote.citation: 1827, Henry Hallam, The Constitutional History of England from the Accession of Henry VII. to the Death of George II. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: John Murray, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: An unconstitutional method of obtaining aid.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “[…] it is not fair of you to bring against mankind double weapons ! Dangerous enough you are as woman alone, without bringing to your aid those gifts of mind suited to problems which men have been accustomed to arrogate to themselves.”

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Tobit 8:6:
quote.text: It is not good that man should bee alone, let vs make vnto him an aide like to himselfe.

definitions.definition: (countable) Something which helps; a material source of help.

quote.citation: 1983, Richard Ellis, The Book of Sharks, Knopf, →ISBN, page 16:
quote.text: The human is so poorly designed for aquatic adventures that he cannot even see in the water without artificial aids.

quote.citation: 2013 September-October, Henry Petroski, “The Evolution of Eyeglasses”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: The ability of a segment of a glass sphere to magnify whatever is placed before it was known around the year 1000, when the spherical segment was called a reading stone […]. Scribes, illuminators, and scholars held such stones directly over manuscript pages as an aid in seeing what was being written, drawn, or read.

definitions.definition: (countable, British) An historical subsidy granted to the crown by Parliament for an extraordinary purpose, such as a war effort.

quote.citation: 2019, Julia Boffey, Henry VII's London in the Great Chronicle, page 71:
quote.text: In this parliament was granted to the king for defence against the Scots two aids and two quindecims, the which two aids did not extend over two quindecims.

definitions.definition: (countable, law) A pecuniary tribute paid by a vassal to his feudal lord on special occasions.

quote.citation: Robert Michael Wills, They Came from the Drain (page 206)
quote.text: Suddenly, the general's aid entered the room and walked in a straight line, coming to a halt in front of the desk, standing at attention, waiting for the general to recognize him, allowing the aid to speak.

definitions.definition: (countable, chiefly in the plural, horse racing) The rider's use of hands, legs, voice, etc. to control the horse.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English aiden, from Old French eider, aider, aidier, from Latin adiuto, frequentative of adiuvō (“assist”, verb).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To provide support to; to further the progress of; to help; to assist.

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii]:
quote.text: You speedy helpers  […]  Appear and aid me in this enterprise.

quote.citation: 2012 May 24, Nathan Rabin, “Film: Reviews: Men In Black 3”, in The Onion AV Club‎[1]:
quote.text: Smith is aided in his quest by an elfin, time-jumping alien with psychic powers played by another Coen brothers veteran, A Serious Man star Michael Stuhlbarg.

definitions.definition: (climbing) To climb with the use of aids such as pitons.

quote.text: Rather than climb into a bottomless off-width crack, we aided an 80-foot A2 to A3 crack to the top of a pedestal. By very tenuous face climbing, we gained entry to the crack, which we followed to a tree beneath the big chimney.
